fields.title: Multimodal models
fields.intro: Study three questions: how to align modalities, how to budget visual evidence, and how to predict states and the consequences of actions.

fields.title: Cross-modal alignment: representations, connectors, and supervision
fields.question: How do images, speech, and text connect to the same task? Does the model learn similarity or learn to generate answers?
fields.takeaway: CLIP uses separate image and text encoders and a paired contrastive objective to learn shared representations for zero-shot classification and retrieval. BLIP-2 freezes the visual encoder and LLM and uses a Q-Former with a small number of queries to extract visual evidence, connecting vision and language generation in stages. Instruction tuning, distillation, reward modeling, and task-specific evaluation change supervision and readout. Track the inputs, objective, and output interface separately.
fields.example: Finding the image that best matches “red umbrella” is a suitable embedding comparison. Reading the second line of small print needs fine visual evidence and a text-output interface. Connecting an image to an LLM does not automatically give it OCR, and compressed visual queries may lose details.
fields.pitfall: Retrieval similarity is not a probability of factual correctness. Matching words does not prove the image was used. Check negative controls such as shuffled images and distinguish natural image–text pairs, speech accents, and video domains. Small-image runs, random fixtures, and public benchmarks support different claims.
fields.reading_order: Start with CLIP's dual encoders, normalization, and contrastive loss. Then read BLIP-2's Q-Former and two-stage connection to distinguish shared embeddings from language generation. Choose later work on instruction tuning, distillation, rewards, or evaluation to match your task.

fields.question: Can a high CLIP retrieval score establish that the model reads all text in an image?
fields.answer: No. Contrastive pairing mainly constrains overall image–text compatibility. Small text needs enough visual resolution, local representations, and decoding supervision. Evaluate OCR or the relevant fine-grained task separately and verify that results change with image content.

fields.title: Visual evidence budgets: tokens, frames, and on-demand revisiting
fields.question: When visual input is too long, which details can be skipped for now, and which need a way to be recovered?
fields.takeaway: StackTok optimizes question relevance under a coverage constraint that changes with budget, switching criteria according to the current shortfall. ViMoD's DART builds persistent coarse representations and keeps mappings to original Fine tokens; TRACE uses the generated prefix to keep or replace active details. The former mainly selects a subset before decoding; the latter supports revisiting evidence as needs change during inference.
fields.example: Listing all objects requires broad image coverage. Comparing a product label afterward requires local detail. If compression permanently deletes label tokens, later reasoning cannot recover them. Recoverable designs can fetch details but must account for Fine KV storage and retrieval. Long video has a similar trade-off between key frames and temporal coverage.
fields.pitfall: Fewer visual tokens do not imply a proportional drop in whole-system memory or latency. Account for the visual encoder, text decoding, cache, and routing. Recoverability is not free. The local StackTok is a reference selector, while ViMoD has real-checkpoint execution and gradient verification. Neither reproduces the paper's capability gains.
fields.reading_order: Start with StackTok's relevance/coverage switching for one-time budget allocation. Then compare ViMoD's Coarse/Fine and HOLD/UPDATE decisions to see why multistep reasoning may need fresh evidence. Choose additional frame selection, width pruning, or visual caching papers according to the bottleneck.

fields.question: If Fine KV is recoverable, can total visual storage count only the Coarse tokens?
fields.answer: No. Coarse is the resident active context; Fine KV and its mapping still require storage. Dynamic recovery also consumes bandwidth and routing compute. Report active attention budget, total cache storage, and end-to-end latency separately.

fields.title: Visual world models: state, generation, and action conditioning
fields.question: Does the model only recognize a scene, or can it predict how an action changes the state?
fields.takeaway: Learning prediction or control representations requires observations, actions, and future states together. LeWAM jointly learns latent future prediction and action flow matching so representation and policy shape each other. Planning uses latent dynamics to evaluate actions. WOVEN organizes generated video transitions as supervision controlled by scene, action, and reasoning type for consequences, causes, and counterfactuals. SWIM asks which state coordinates should contribute to latent distance. Offline inverse dynamics gates only future displacement; once frozen, sqrt(g) calibrates distances between same-frame pairs. Planning does not read future states.
fields.example: Pushing a cup left and right on the same table should lead to different outcomes. Recognizing a cup does not control a robot. Latent prediction can avoid pixel reconstruction, but test whether actions matter, whether multistep rollouts drift, and whether selected actions reach goals in closed loop.
fields.pitfall: Realistic videos, low one-step error, or high training-set QA scores do not prove effective planning. Separate source scenes and trajectories by group and prevent counterfactuals from leaking future results. Local LeWAM is a non-held-out closed-loop diagnostic; WOVEN is a small experiment on public training data. Neither establishes the paper's full generalization or robotics claims.
fields.reading_order: Start with LeWAM's joint latent and action objective to see how prediction feeds control. Then read WOVEN on visual transitions and controlled supervision. Distinguish representation learning, synthetic data, question answering, and closed-loop planning. Follow up with visual geometry, video memory, or embodied actions.

fields.question: Does lower one-step latent MSE necessarily improve long-horizon control success?
fields.answer: No. Errors can fall in directions irrelevant to action choice, compound over a rollout, or be exploited by policy search. Compare closed-loop control with matched environments, goals, and budgets, and do not present training trajectories as held out.
